When you call something godforsaken, you are saying it is so bleak, miserable, and cut off from anything good that it feels as if even God has turned His back on it and walked away. It is a word that captures a deep sense of abandonment, wretchedness, and hopelessness — all packed into one sharp, expressive word.

Think of it as combining two feelings at once: this place is terrible + this place feels completely forgotten by the world.

Godforsaken is used almost exclusively to describe places — and occasionally situations or times. It is rarely used to describe a person directly in modern English.

When you use it to describe a place, you are usually saying that the place is:

  • Remote and isolated — far from civilization, far from anything useful or comforting. Miles and miles from the nearest town, hospital, or decent road.
  • Bleak and depressing — not just empty, but unpleasantly empty. Cold, grey, lifeless, dull. A place that drains the spirit just by looking at it.
  • Lacking any redeeming quality — there is nothing interesting, enjoyable, or worthwhile about it. You cannot find a single reason to be glad you are there.

"Why did they send me to work in this godforsaken desert town? There's nothing here but dust and flies."

"The cabin was stuck in some godforsaken corner of the mountains where your phone got no signal and the heating didn't work."

In both examples, notice that the place is not just bad — it feels like it has been forgotten by the rest of the world. That sense of abandonment is the heart of the word.
The Emotional Colour of the Word

This is not a neutral, clinical word. It is charged with strong feeling — usually frustration, despair, or contempt. When someone calls a place godforsaken, they are not calmly stating a fact. They are venting. They are expressing how wretched they feel about being there.

Because of this, the word is:

  • Informal — you would say it in conversation or casual writing, not in a formal report or academic essay.
  • Somewhat dramatic — it is an exaggeration (a hyperbole). The speaker does not literally believe God has abandoned the place. They are using the word for emotional emphasis, the way someone might say "I'm dying of boredom" without literally dying.
  • Mildly strong in tone — it is not a swear word, but it is forceful. It is the kind of word you use when you really want to make your displeasure clear.

You might wonder: why not just say a place is terrible or awful? Here is the distinction:

  • Terrible just means very bad.
  • Godforsaken means very bad in a specific way — isolated, abandoned, bleak, devoid of life or comfort, as if the world has left it behind entirely.

A loud, crowded, chaotic city might be terrible, but you would not call it godforsaken — it has too much life and presence. Godforsaken implies emptiness, desolation, and a feeling of being cut off. That is its special flavour.
Can It Describe Situations or Times?

Yes, occasionally. If someone calls a situation or period of time godforsaken, they mean it was utterly miserable, hopeless, and without comfort — much the same feeling applied to an experience rather than a location.

"Those were the most godforsaken years of my life — unemployed, alone, and stuck in a grey little flat."

Here, the speaker is not just saying those years were bad. They are saying those years felt bleak, abandoned, and without hope — as if grace and good fortune had completely deserted them.

One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine you are a traveller who has taken a wrong turn and ended up in a crumbling, windswept, cold little village in the middle of nowhere. There are no shops open. No one on the streets. The sky is grey. Your car has broken down. You look around and think: "What kind of place is this? It feels like the whole world — and God himself — has forgotten this place even exists."

That feeling? That is exactly what godforsaken captures.
